Business Compatibility: Complete Content Page 1
Business Compatibility: Complete Content (checked against
online sources)
What was checked online, and what was not. Please read this first.
CONFIRMED from sources: (1) The ruler of each 10 day part of a sign (decan) follows the Chaldean order, as given by
Ptolemy and Lilly. Checked on Wikipedia (Decan), Astro.com (traditional astrology options) and Kerykeion (Face and
Decan). Aries is Mars, Sun, Venus; Taurus is Mercury, Moon, Saturn; and so on for all 36 parts. There is a second, modern
method (by triplicity, spread in the 20th century by Alan Leo), and many modern astrologers use it. This file uses the
traditional Chaldean method.
CONFIRMED from sources: (2) The trades each planet rules come from William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), in the
adapted text on Skyscript by Deborah Houlding. For example Mars: soldiers, surgeons, smiths, bakers, cooks, carpenters.
Moon: sailors, fishermen, brewers, nurses, carriers. Mercury: writers, merchants, schoolmasters, attorneys, clerks,
printers. Venus: musicians, painters, tailors, jewellers, perfumers. Jupiter: judges, lawyers, clergy, students. Saturn:
farmers, miners, potters, plumbers, gardeners. Sun: rulers, magistrates, stewards, goldsmiths, minters.
PARTLY CONFIRMED: (3) The careers linked to each sign come from modern astrology articles (Bustle, Marie Claire,
Blavity, ZipRecruiter and similar). They are lifestyle sources, not classical books, but they agree on most points, for
example finance and real estate for the earth signs, health and care work for the water signs, and communication and
technology for the air signs. Where they differed I kept the overlap.
NOT from any book, my own design: the 3 day split, the percentage formula, the weights, how the planet trades were
matched to the 35 business categories of the app (for example Lilly's smiths became Chemicals, Metals and Machinery),
and all the written texts. An astrologer may adjust these.
Dates. Sources differ by a day on sign boundaries (for example Capricorn starts on 21 or 22 December). The standard
ranges used are Aries 21 March to 19 April, and so on, as in the group tables.
Astrology is not scientifically proven to predict business success. Please show users a short note that results are guidance
and not a promise.
Placeholders: [%] is the percentage, [business] is the role selected by the user, [option1], [option2], [option3] are the top
three categories of the user's date group. Match levels: High is 80 to 97, Mid is 65 to 79, Low is 52 to 64. No text the user
reads mentions a sign or a date.

Low match: Q1. What Makes Your Business Compatibility [%]?
The score of [%] shows a gap between your courage and the detailed demands of [business].

Low match: Q2. Best Business Options for Your Success
A score of [%] means [business] will be an uphill climb, so plan with care.
Your courage is better used in [option1] or [option2], where you meet less resistance.
Consider moving to [option3], which fits your initiative better.
If you still want [business], run it as a side project and bring in a partner for the leadership part.
Do not risk your main savings here, and build your base in your strongest option first.
Business Growth plan (2 months)
Month 1, Week 1: Define your offer and your money base
Step 1
Write your offer in one bold sentence that says what you sell and who it helps.
Choose the customer who can say yes fastest.
Choose a bold and specific offer, since your inner drive works best with a clear target.
Line 4 (High): Because your match is strong, aim your offer at the exact kind of work where your natural skills show most.
Line 4 (Mid): Because your match is good, include one extra skill or helper that covers what comes less easily to you.
Line 4 (Low): Because your match is lower, keep this first offer very small so you can learn with little risk.
Step 2
Open a simple record of money in and money out on day one.
Set a spending limit for the week and stay inside it.
Set a strict spending limit and hold to it, because impulsive spending is your main money risk.
Line 4 (High): Your strong fit lets you plan with confidence, but still keep a cash reserve for slow weeks.
Line 4 (Mid): Keep a slightly larger reserve than usual, as the learning period may cost more time.
Line 4 (Low): Keep costs as low as possible and avoid loans or big purchases in these first weeks.
Month 1, Week 2: Win first customers and set quality
Step 1
Contact customers directly by call or visit, since your energy sells better than long messages.
Ask for a clear yes or no in each conversation.
Go after customers directly and follow up quickly, as speed is your advantage.
Line 4 (High): Aim for steady early sales, since your natural fit should help you win trust quickly.
Line 4 (Mid): Aim for a few honest sales and note where customers hesitate so you can improve.
Line 4 (Low): Aim for a handful of trial customers and ask openly what is missing from your offer.
Business Compatibility: Complete Content Page 4
Step 2
Decide the exact standard of your service and check it every time.
Your speed can cause small mistakes, so use a short checklist before each delivery.
Give every order the same full effort, even when you feel in a hurry.
Line 4 (High): Protect the high quality your fit makes possible and write down exactly how you achieve it.
Line 4 (Mid): Check each delivery carefully, since the harder parts of this work need extra attention from you.
Line 4 (Low): Have an experienced person review your first deliveries so mistakes are caught early.
Month 1, Week 3: Become visible and listen
Step 1
Pick one channel and post or speak about your business every day.
Use short strong messages with one clear action for the customer.
Be direct and confident in your message, and show your strongest result first.
Line 4 (High): Put more effort into the channel that brings your best customers and cut the weaker ones.
Line 4 (Mid): Test two channels for a full week each and keep only the one that brings real buyers.
Line 4 (Low): Use one low cost channel only and learn from its results before spending anything more.
Step 2
Call or message each customer after the sale to ask how it went.
Listen fully before you answer or defend yourself.
Take criticism as training and answer it with action instead of defending yourself.
Line 4 (High): Ask happy customers for reviews so your strong results become visible proof.
Line 4 (Mid): Ask every customer one question about what could be better and act on the pattern.
Line 4 (Low): Treat every complaint as a lesson and use it to decide whether this path really suits you.
Month 1, Week 4: Review the first month
Step 1
Count sales, costs and profit for the month in one sheet.
Mark your best and worst results.
Measure what you finished and not what you started to see your true progress.
Line 4 (High): Compare your numbers with your goal and raise the goal if you are ahead.
Line 4 (Mid): Compare your numbers with your goal and adjust the plan if you are slightly behind.
Line 4 (Low): Compare your numbers honestly and decide whether to continue, change or add a second option.
Step 2
Choose the single biggest problem and solve it before starting anything new.
Your habit of jumping ahead can leave old problems open.
Attack the hardest problem first while your energy is high.
Line 4 (High): Fix small leaks quickly so they do not slow a business that is already working well.
Line 4 (Mid): Fix the problem that wastes the most time, since this is where your effort is being lost.
Line 4 (Low): Fix the problem or step back from it, and do not spend more until the cause is clear.
Month 2, Week 5: Build systems and support
Business Compatibility: Complete Content Page 5
Step 1
Plan a fixed daily schedule with selling in your most energetic hours.
Keep routine tasks in a short block so they do not drain you.
Use your high energy hours for the hardest work and keep rest inside the plan.
Line 4 (High): Turn what works into written steps so your results become easy to repeat.
Line 4 (Mid): Write steps for the tasks that are difficult for you so they stop depending on mood.
Line 4 (Low): Write clear steps for every task so that you are not relying on instinct alone.
Step 2
Find one patient person who can handle details and paperwork.
Give clear tasks with deadlines and trust them to finish.
Pick helpers who can work at your pace but who can also slow you down when you rush.
Line 4 (High): Add a helper only for tasks that free you to do your strongest work.
Line 4 (Mid): Add a helper or advisor who is strong where you feel less certain.
Line 4 (Low): Find a partner or mentor who already succeeds in this field and learn from them.
Month 2, Week 6: Grow sales and keep customers
Step 1
Set a weekly sales target slightly above last week.
Try one new customer group or area and watch the numbers.
Push for growth in short sprints with a clear target for each one.
Line 4 (High): Use your strong fit to raise prices or offers gradually, since demand should support it.
Line 4 (Mid): Increase sales through one new offer or area at a time and watch the results.
Line 4 (Low): Grow only if the numbers are steady, and consider testing a better matched option beside it.
Step 2
Offer repeat customers a simple reward for returning.
Keep in touch after the sale with a short message.
Show customers you are reliable by fixing problems quickly and without arguing.
Line 4 (High): Reward loyal customers so your best relationships turn into steady monthly income.
Line 4 (Mid): Follow up with every buyer so first sales become repeat sales.
Line 4 (Low): Focus on keeping the few customers you have, since they are your best source of learning.
Month 2, Week 7: Protect profit and reduce risk
Step 1
Set aside a fixed share of every sale for savings and taxes.
Check your cash balance every Friday.
Control sudden big purchases, because your bold side can spend faster than you earn.
Line 4 (High): Save a fixed share of profit now so that your growth is paid for from your own income.
Line 4 (Mid): Keep your profit margin clear and cut costs that do not bring customers.
Line 4 (Low): Watch cash every week and do not borrow, because patience is safer than pressure.
Business Compatibility: Complete Content Page 6
Step 2
List the three things that could stop your business, such as a late supplier or a lost customer.
Prepare one backup for each.
Guard against burnout by planning real days of rest.
Line 4 (High): Protect your strong position with simple backups, such as a second supplier or saved copies of records.
Line 4 (Mid): Prepare for the weak points of this work by keeping a plan for slow weeks and mistakes.
Line 4 (Low): Keep a stop limit, which is a clear amount of money or time you will not exceed without proof of progress.
Month 2, Week 8: Review and plan the long term
Step 1
Look back over two months and list your three best results.
Write the mistakes that cost you most, usually rushing.
Set a challenging goal and divide it into small battles you can win each week.
Line 4 (High): Set a bigger goal for the next stage, since your fit supports real expansion.
Line 4 (Mid): Set a balanced goal and continue building the skills that are still developing.
Line 4 (Low): Decide with your numbers whether to continue, improve or shift toward a better matched field.
Step 2
Keep a weekly review of numbers and a monthly goal.
Stay with plans until they finish before starting new ones.
Keep a steady pace for the long run, because endurance wins more than bursts of energy.
Line 4 (High): Keep the weekly habits that created your success, because consistency matters most when things go well.
Line 4 (Mid): Keep your weekly review so that small problems never grow into large ones.
Line 4 (Low): Keep a monthly review and be ready to adjust your direction as you learn more about yourself.

Line 4 (High): Because your match is strong, aim your offer at the exact kind of work where your natural skills show most.
Line 4 (Mid): Because your match is good, include one extra skill or helper that covers what comes less easily to you.
Line 4 (Low): Because your match is lower, keep this first offer very small so you can learn with little risk.
Step 2
Set a strict record system for all money and keep a reserve.
Review it weekly.
Set a strict spending limit and hold to it, because impulsive spending is your main money risk.
Line 4 (High): Your strong fit lets you plan with confidence, but still keep a cash reserve for slow weeks.
Line 4 (Mid): Keep a slightly larger reserve than usual, as the learning period may cost more time.
Line 4 (Low): Keep costs as low as possible and avoid loans or big purchases in these first weeks.
Month 1, Week 2: Win first customers and set quality
Step 1

Line 4 (Mid): Aim for a few honest sales and note where customers hesitate so you can improve.
Line 4 (Low): Aim for a handful of trial customers and ask openly what is missing from your offer.

Line 4 (Mid): Check each delivery carefully, since the harder parts of this work need extra attention from you.
Line 4 (Low): Have an experienced person review your first deliveries so mistakes are caught early.
Month 1, Week 3: Become visible and listen
Step 1

Line 4 (High): Put more effort into the channel that brings your best customers and cut the weaker ones.

Line 4 (Low): Use one low cost channel only and learn from its results before spending anything more.

Line 4 (High): Ask happy customers for reviews so your strong results become visible proof.

Line 4 (Low): Treat every complaint as a lesson and use it to decide whether this path really suits you.

Step 1

Line 4 (Low): Compare your numbers honestly and decide whether to continue, change or add a second option.

Business compatibility content
121 groups, 35 categories, 190 roles. Every group has its own Question 1 and Question 2 text for four match levels.
Placeholders in square brackets are filled by the app from the selected category and role.
How the score works
Top five categories in each group keep the scores from your source file. All other categories and every role get a fixed score
from the same formula, so the same input always gives the same result. Levels: 80 and above strong, 65 to 79 good, 50 to 64
uphill, below 50 not really worth it. Question 1 shows two roles only: the one selected and the role in the same category with
the nearest score. The best options in Question 2 come from the five curated categories of each group.
Placeholders
[role] [score] [demand1] [demand2] [optionA] [optionB] [optionC] [roleA] [roleB] [roleC]. Options skip the category the user
selected.
